They're sponsoring another video" — the read lands AFTER the payoff, when viewers feel released. 4 · how (the next move)Move the read to 5:38-5:50, tease the daybed verdict, run Quince, then deliver "I like them a lot better" as the post-ad payoff. 5 · rationaleSponsor reads hold at the height of anticipation, not after release; the current placement burns 9,472 viewers where the channel norm predicts about 1,900. cautionVerify Quince's contract permits repositioning and a mid-verdict cut; if locked, A/B a shorter 15-second version in the same slot and measure stop rate against 5.38%.
peak7:29

peak7:53

drop18:48

drop0:00

drop10:16

The "art" vs "design" of getting dressed

published 2025-02-13 · analysed 2026-09-01

1 · Retention breakdown

curve100 samples, stored one per percent runtime14:35 gone by 0:3032% at halfway41% still watching methodhazard = (present before − present after) ÷ present before at each moment; baseline = mean hazard of the previous 5 moments, floored; flagged when the excess viewers lost beyond baseline ranks high; a rise is a rewind only when no comparable drop precedes it and the lift survives the next sample

Red marks are flagged drops, green are earned rewinds. Hover a mark for its note.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:00
1 · what the curve showedThe opening nine seconds shed the usual first-frame chunk, slightly heavier than the channel handles it (*10.55% stop rate vs 8.54% typical, 2,227 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“where does this interest fall” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The premise question is posed before any payoff: "where does this interest fall" — an abstract framing rather than a concrete hook. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load one styled outfit reveal or a concrete art-vs-design contrast before the question is asked at 0:05. 5 · rationaleOpening loss runs +5.2pp above the channel median, so the hook is underperforming this creator's own norm rather than a universal cliff.
drop0:35
1 · what the curve showedA secondary bleed lands the moment the sponsor is named, running 1.4x the channel norm at this position (*2.50% vs 1.73%, 777 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“thank the sponsor of this video” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The sponsor handoff arrives before any content has been delivered: "thank the sponsor of this video which is once again level eight luggage". 4 · how (the next move)Trial moving the level eight read to roughly 2:30, after the artist-vs-designer question is teased but before the answer. 5 · rationaleAds hold best at the height of anticipation; running the read before the premise is even stated releases viewers with nothing owed them. cautionVerify the sponsor contract permits repositioning the read past the one-minute mark; if it locks placement, tighten the read instead.
peak1:36
1 · what the curve showedThe audience rebuilds by 8.5% and holds for 13 samples as the sponsor read winds down (*529 viewers regained, audience at 56.3%*). 2 · evidence at that second“thank you so much again to level 8” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub back to the pivot out of the ad: "thank you so much again to level 8 for sponsoring this video" immediately precedes the topic tease. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:35-1:38 down to a 20-second read and land the "for some reason I've been thinking lately" pivot by 1:00. 5 · rationaleThe rebuild proves the topic pulls people back; the run-up to it is what shed them, so shortening the gap keeps the audience that currently rewinds to find it.
drop1:54
1 · what the curve showedStop rate here is actually half the channel norm and the audience rises through the window (*0.65% vs 1.42% typical, 0.5x*), so this is not a drop to act on. 2 · evidence at that second“the differences between Art and Design” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The premise finally lands in plain terms: "the differences between Art and Design and where my mindset is" — viewers lean in as the topic clarifies. 4 · how (the next move)Preserve the 1:43-2:22 framing beat verbatim in future edits; use it as the template for how this channel should open topic videos. 5 · rationaleThe flagged spike ratio reflects the recovery off the sponsor trough, not fresh loss — the segment is doing the work the intro should have done.
peak1:54
1 · what the curve showedA second, shorter rebuild adds 4.9% of the present audience as the premise is named (*332 viewers regained, held for 3 samples, audience at 59.7%*). 2 · evidence at that second“wear the hat of an artist or of a designer” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The artist-vs-designer framing crystallises here: "wear the hat of an artist or of a designer" — the concrete question viewers came for. 4 · how (the next move)Reuse this exact phrasing in the thumbnail text or opening line so the hook and the rebuild point say the same thing. 5 · rationaleTwo consecutive replay peaks landing on the same framing show this is the sentence viewers are hunting for; putting it earlier removes the hunt.

drop0:00

peak2:42

drop2:57

drop6:09

peak16:13
1 · what the curve showedAudience climbs mid-video as she articulates a self-diagnostic for personal style (*audience rose 3.5%, 259 regained*). 2 · evidence at that second“apart from and separated from being chronically online” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)She names how offline excitement about a boring item reveals genuine taste separate from online fashion discourse. 4 · how (the next move)Expand this thought into a standalone video on finding personal style outside online trend cycles. 5 · rationaleA replay peak on a framework, not an outfit, signals an idea the audience wants developed at length.
peak20:38
1 · what the curve showedA late replay peak lands on a tonal-dressing observation (*audience rose 2.3%, 144 regained at 31.9% still present*). 2 · evidence at that second“have them all be the same shade” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)She unpacks why matching every loose piece to one shade of beige makes an overwhelming outfit visually digestible. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load a tonal-dressing breakdown into the first third of the next styling video. 5 · rationaleViewers rewound for a concrete styling rule with a visible before/after logic, the strongest teachable moment in the video.

Avoiding Trends = Understyling

published 2024-10-22 · analysed 2026-09-01

1 · Retention breakdown

curve100 samples, stored one per percent runtime11:16 gone by 0:3028% at halfway54% still watching methodhazard = (present before − present after) ÷ present before at each moment; baseline = mean hazard of the previous 5 moments, floored; flagged when the excess viewers lost beyond baseline ranks high; a rise is a rewind only when no comparable drop precedes it and the lift survives the next sample

Red marks are flagged drops, green are earned rewinds. Hover a mark for its note.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:00
1 · what the curve showedThe first seven seconds shed viewers slower than this channel usually does at the open (*6.65% stop rate vs the channel's 8.54% here, 815 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“I feel like that's me right now” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The cold open frames the premise as a personal admission — 'possible to have a good fashion sense while lacking style and I feel like that's me right now' — instead of branding or greeting. 4 · how (the next move)Keep this cold open intact and model future intros on its structure: premise-as-confession before any music sting or channel branding. 5 · rationaleThe 30-second mark beats 146 of 148 channel videos, so whatever this opening does is the channel's best working template.
peak1:14
1 · what the curve showedA small early rewind lands on the simplicity qualifier (*+1.8% of audience present, 63 viewers regained, 70.6% still watching*). 2 · evidence at that second“I love simple outfits when they're intentional” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The line 'I have no problem with Simplicity I love simple outfits when they're intentional' is the thesis distinction viewers scrub back to catch. 4 · how (the next move)Repeat this intentional-versus-boring-simple distinction as a spoken chapter title around 1:10 in future style-diagnosis videos. 5 · rationaleThe rewind proves this is the sentence viewers wanted to re-hear — surfacing it as a marker makes the payoff findable without scrubbing.
peak7:40
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises and holds across two samples on the Charleston observation (*+3.2% of audience present, 80 viewers regained, held for 2 samples*). 2 · evidence at that second“styles that I claim to hate or would never wear myself” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The beat lands a concrete observation about a real place — 'styles that I claim to hate or would never wear myself still bring me so much more joy'. 4 · how (the next move)Expand this Charleston-and-Sunshine-Coast observation into its own standalone video on places that changed how she reads style. 5 · rationaleA two-sample hold is the video's strongest sustained interest signal, and the material is location-anchored enough to carry a full runtime.
drop8:20
1 · what the curve showedViewers leave at twice the channel's rate for this position, on the same beat where others scrub back (*2.0x channel norm, 5.8x surrounding stop rate, 175 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“I would never wear an outfit like this or this or this” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The line 'I would never wear an outfit like this or this or this' cues visual examples the audio-only listener cannot follow, splitting the audience. 4 · how (the next move)Cut the three unnamed 'this or this or this' references and replace with one named example viewers can picture without seeing the screen. 5 · rationaleThe same moment is a replay peak, so the idea works — the loss is viewers who cannot access the visual reference stack. cautionThis assumes the three referenced looks are not a load-bearing visual gag; if the on-screen contrast is the joke, trial the cut on one upload first.
peak8:20
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises here as viewers scrub back to the Lily Pulitzer beat (*+3.4% of audience present, 90 viewers regained, 54.4% still watching*). 2 · evidence at that second“I claim to hate Lily Pitzer for example” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The moment names a specific brand as a personal contradiction — 'I claim to hate Lily Pitzer for example but when I see girls dressed up' — which viewers rewind to catch. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load one named-brand contradiction like this one into the first two minutes of future videos on personal taste. 5 · rationaleNamed specificity is what earned the rewind — the abstract framing earlier in the video did not generate the same behaviour.
drop10:15
1 · what the curve showedThe subscribe ask triggers a drop nearly twice the channel's norm for this position (*1.9x channel norm, 5.05% stop rate, 181 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“subscribe to my channel and we will be in this together” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The ask lands after the thesis has resolved — 'subscribe to my channel and we will be in this together' — releasing viewers who felt the video was over. 4 · how (the next move)Move the subscribe ask to 9:53 before 'sometimes it takes learning a lesson in five different roundabout ways', while the reflection is still building. 5 · rationaleAds and asks hold best at the height of anticipation, not after the payoff — the current placement sits exactly on the release beat.

drop0:00

peak2:25
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 9.8% mid-segment and holds for 23 samples, the strongest sustained rewatch in the video (*10 viewers regained, 44.8% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“classless chaps on Spotify Apple podcast” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)She names the podcast and platforms: 'classless chaps on Spotify Apple podcast', then teases a rebrand and a March launch date — concrete info viewers scrub back to catch. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load the podcast name, platforms and March date into a titled card in the first minute so new viewers get the info without hunting. 5 · rationaleA 23-sample hold on a specific name-and-date drop shows this is reference-seeking behaviour, not enjoyment — surfacing it earlier serves the same intent without the scrub.
peak2:31
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 7.3% but only holds two samples before falling back (*8 viewers regained, 48.1% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“podcast should be up by the end of March” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Overlaps the same podcast announcement: 'the first podcast should be up by the end of March' — the release date itself is what viewers scrubbed to hear. 4 · how (the next move)Merge this beat with the 2:25 fix: put the March release date on the same early card so both scrub-backs are pre-empted together. 5 · rationaleA two-sample hold is a check-and-leave — viewers grabbed the date and moved on, confirming the podcast info is reference material, not narrative.
peak3:53
1 · what the curve showedAudience climbs 8.3% around the haircut reveal and holds nine samples (*9 viewers regained, 45.5% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“that girl has a CH yeah” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The exchange 'that girl has a CH yeah but not by not buy a lot yeah no that's fine' lands on the moment the cut length is decided — a visible result viewers replay. 4 · how (the next move)Show the finished haircut in a tight before/after cutaway immediately after 3:53 so the payoff reads on first watch, not only on rewind. 5 · rationaleA nine-sample hold on a styling decision means viewers want to see the outcome — making the result visible in-line converts the replay into forward watch time.
drop4:25
1 · what the curve showedA 32-second stretch drops audience from 48.1% to 39.0%, but the stop rate barely exceeds the channel's usual behaviour here (*6.8x spike, 19 viewers lost, 1.1x channel norm*). 2 · evidence at that second“I forgot how tiring photo shoots” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A hard scene change from the haircut ('I'm proud of us yeah me too') into a next-morning talking head about pimple patches and 'homemade photo shoot' recap. 4 · how (the next move)Trial cutting 4:41-4:53's morning-after preamble and open the new scene on the photoshoot itself, keeping the pimple-patch aside as a later aside. 5 · rationaleThe loss tracks the channel's own habit at this position, so the priority is testing whether removing the recap language holds the transition, not surgery on the scene. cautionThe morning-after frame may set up later photoshoot payoffs; verify the following segment still reads without it before committing the cut.
drop9:46

drop0:00

peak14:57

1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 2.8% at the shift from deliberation into rapid-fire sorting (*5 viewers regained, 44.8% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“okay rapid fire keeping these” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub to the pace change — "okay rapid fire keeping these these I love" — the first moment decisions come faster than justifications. 4 · how (the next move)Move a rapid-fire block into the first four minutes and use the slower deliberations as breaks between them. 5 · rationaleThe only three replays in a 23-minute video all sit on structure or pace shifts, not items — the current edit buries its most-rewound mode past the midpoint.
peak12:57
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 5.1% and holds for four samples around the bathroom transition (*8 viewers regained, 43.0% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“we'll tackle my bathroom and like accessories” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub back to the room-change beat — "we'll tackle my bathroom and like accessories" — the clearest chapter marker in the video. 4 · how (the next move)Add an on-screen room-title card at each new zone (closet, bathroom, accessories) and mirror this cadence in future decluttering videos. 5 · rationaleThe replay proves viewers use room transitions as navigation anchors; making them visible reduces the need to scrub.
drop13:11
1 · what the curve showedA 56-second window loses 12 viewers and drops audience from 44.3% to 40.5%, running 1.7x the channel norm and flagged as unusual for this channel (*7.3x surrounding stop rate*). 2 · evidence at that second“my hair appointment got canceled” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The creator announces a break for a hair appointment, cuts, then returns saying "my hair appointment got canceled so you're stuck with my dirty hair" — a false exit that reads as end-of-segment. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 12:46-13:10 entirely and jump straight from the giveaway bag to "I'm going to tackle the bathroom cabinet". 5 · rationaleThis is one of the few moments genuinely worse than the channel's habit, and the cancelled-appointment beat gives viewers a natural exit for no narrative gain.
peak13:11
1 · what the curve showedA second smaller replay lifts audience 3.0% right as the reverse-packing rule is stated (*5 viewers regained, 44.3% present*). 2 · evidence at that second“I'm basically reverse packing” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to catch the method — "I'm basically reverse packing like I'm only keeping what I'm going to pack" — the one explicit framework in the episode. 4 · how (the next move)Pull the reverse-packing definition to the top of the video as the stated method, and restate it once per room transition. 5 · rationaleThe rewind shows this line does organising work for viewers; surfacing it earlier gives the whole sort a spine the current cut lacks.

1 · what the curve showedA short spike at the halfway mark loses 4.8 points of a thinning audience (*6.0x surrounding stop rate, 4.0x channel norm, 8 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“fitted long sleeve bodysuits” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)One cashmere-zip prediction ends and another begins with no transition — "fitted long sleeve bodysuits" is announced flat over silence at 7:34. 4 · how (the next move)Cut the 7:34 silence and add a one-line stakes tease before "fitted long sleeve bodysuits," naming what era it unlocks. 5 · rationaleChannel-typical loss here is 1.01%; this video ran 4.07%, so the item-to-item handoff, not the prediction itself, is where viewers release.
peak7:35
1 · what the curve showedA one-sample lift of 9.7% coincides with the same moment flagged as a drop (*7 viewers regained, audience 40.5%*). 2 · evidence at that second“fitted long sleeve bodysuits” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A handful rewind to catch "fitted long sleeve bodysuits specifically paired with high-waisted jeans and a belt" — a concrete outfit prescription — while more leave. 4 · how (the next move)Trial adding an on-screen outfit still at 7:37 so the prescription is scannable without rewinding, and pair it with the drop-side transition fix. 5 · rationaleThe rewind and the drop share a timestamp, so the specific outfit line is worth surfacing visually rather than losing it inside the audio segue. cautionHeld for only one sample, so the rewind signal is thin; keep the change only if the 7:35 stop rate falls back toward the 1.01% channel norm.
drop12:32
1 · what the curve showedThe pivot into the beauty section drops 4.4 points, well above the channel's late-video norm (*5.4x surrounding stop rate, 2.7x channel norm, 7 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“to round out my predictions” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A wrap-up phrase signals the video is closing — "to round out my predictions I'll talk a little bit more about beauty" — releasing viewers before the beauty picks land. 4 · how (the next move)Cut "to round out my predictions" and hard-cut from the perms line straight into "powdered makeup look is gonna come back." 5 · rationaleChannel norm here is 1.08%; this video hit 2.95%, and the wrap-up cue is the only new element separating the two segments.

drop0:00

drop8:53

1 · Retention breakdown

curve100 samples, stored one per percent runtime35:53 gone by 0:3055.6% at halfway25% still watching methodhazard = (present before − present after) ÷ present before at each moment; baseline = mean hazard of the previous 5 moments, floored; flagged when the excess viewers lost beyond baseline ranks high; a rise is a rewind only when no comparable drop precedes it and the lift survives the next sample

Red marks are flagged drops, green are earned rewinds. Hover a mark for its note.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:00
1 · what the curve showedHalf the audience walks out between 0:15 and 0:30, collapsing from 95.8% to 49.0% (*1.6x the channel's stop rate here, 98 viewers lost*). 2 · evidence at that second“sat down at my gate” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The cold open is a teary airport story that never names the video's promise, opening on "sat down at my gate in LA and just started bawling" before pivoting to a detained-in-the-airport tangent. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 0:00-0:22 and open on a hard list promise naming three specific things she didn't expect, then cue the airport cry as evidence. 5 · rationale0:15 beats 142 of 148 channel videos, but 0:30 beats only 13 of 148 — the loss is triggered by what follows the emotional cold open, not the hook itself.
drop9:41
1 · what the curve showedA list of Australian slang words triggers a 4.1x channel-norm exit at the 28% mark (*29.7x the surrounding stop rate, 15 viewers lost*). 2 · evidence at that second“misso servo the tip togs” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The segment turns into a rapid-fire vocabulary dump — "misso servo the tip togs Bogan Chuck Esky Sanger" — with no story or payoff attached to any term. 4 · how (the next move)Cut the list-of-words stretch from 9:48 to 10:01 and keep only the arvo anecdote, then move straight into the how-long-have-you-been-here beat. 5 · rationaleStop rate quadruples the channel norm here, and the anecdote before the list holds fine — the naked word list is what breaks the pace.
drop25:50
1 · what the curve showedThe visa segment loses 5.9 points of remaining audience across 43 seconds (*5.6x the channel norm, 12 viewers lost*), even as others rewind into it. 2 · evidence at that second“ungodly number of hours and dollars” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)She names the topic then vents rather than explains — "the Visa residency citizenship situation is so complicated" — with a 17-second gap of dead air from 25:58 to 26:15. 4 · how (the next move)Cut the 25:58-26:15 silence and replace the vent with one concrete visa story — the flight anecdote she teases at 26:19 — before the Home Affairs complaint. 5 · rationaleThis same timestamp is the video's top replay peak (20.7% rose), so the topic pulls interest; the drop is the delivery, not the subject.
peak25:50
1 · what the curve showedThe visa segment pulls the strongest rewind in the video (*20.7% of the audience present, 11 viewers regained*) at the 72% mark. 2 · evidence at that second“surely you can just get citizenship” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers scrub back to the setup question "surely you can just get citizenship," which frames the single most searchable practical stake in the video. 4 · how (the next move)Cut a standalone video titled around the visa/citizenship question and open it with this exact framing, then link it from this timestamp. 5 · rationaleA replay peak stacked on top of the biggest late drop means the topic is in demand but the delivery is not — a dedicated video separates the two problems.
peak29:25
1 · what the curve showedThe permanent-residency workaround beat holds three samples up (*8.4% rose, 4 viewers regained*) at the 82% mark. 2 · evidence at that second“lying to get sponsored” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to the concrete escape routes — "partnership Visa" and people "lying to get sponsored" — which are the first specific answers in the visa segment. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load these two concrete routes into the 25:50 visa segment before any venting, so the specifics arrive with the topic. 5 · rationaleThe same audience that quits at 25:50 rewinds four minutes later for specifics — delivering them earlier converts the drop into a hold.
peak31:56

1 · what the curve showedAudience climbs to 123.9% of those present and holds for 15 samples, regaining 52 viewers at 23.9% total audience. 2 · evidence at that second“at its best it gives Rachel Green” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind to the pre-salon setup where she frames the stakes — "at its best it gives Rachel Green at its worst it gives grandma". 4 · how (the next move)Front-load this Rachel-Green/grandma framing into the first 30 seconds as the promise of the video. 5 · rationaleA 15-sample hold means viewers are actively scrubbing back to this line, so it is the strongest premise the video already contains.
peak18:03

drop19:32
1 · what the curve showedThe reveal window loses audience from 48.1% down to 17.4% across 64 seconds (*2.9x the channel norm, 78 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“I think I really like it I really think” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)The reveal is immediately followed by hedged self-review — "I think I really like it I really think that I do" — and logistics about kneeling on the floor. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 19:39-20:36 and end on the first clean reveal frame at 19:36 with the line "it is most certainly red". 5 · rationaleViewers came for the transformation; extending past the payoff with commentary is exactly where anticipation releases and they leave.
peak19:32

drop0:00

1 · what the curve showedA 36-second stretch late in the video sheds audience from 31.1% to 24.2% (*4.4x the channel norm here, 8 viewers*). 2 · evidence at that second“very full circle moment to end out the day” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)A pole session montage ends and Phoebe pivots to a reflective monologue: "this was a very full circle moment to end out the day" — the action stops and a caveat-laden aside begins. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 17:06-17:24 and rejoin on the substantive pole reflection after "I don't have a dance background" so the monologue starts with content, not hedging. 5 · rationaleThe stop rate here is 5.68% against a 1.30% channel norm — the disclaimers about being "not really a beginner" and "not like amazing" are where viewers leave.
peak16:59
1 · what the curve showedA small replay lifts audience to 31.1%, with 4.7% of viewers scrubbing back but holding only 1 sample (*2 viewers regained*). 2 · evidence at that second“look at that it's beautiful” (transcript) 3 · why (the check or the quote)Viewers rewind into the pole session montage — "look at that" and "it's beautiful" over music — to re-watch the trick, then leave as the monologue begins. 4 · how (the next move)Extend the pole footage by 10-15 seconds before cutting to the reflective monologue, so the rewatched moment has room to breathe. 5 · rationaleThe peak holds for only 1 sample and the same timestamp is the video's worst late drop — viewers came back for the doing, not the talking about it.

thrifting & antiquing in three different towns

published 1970-01-01 · analysed 2026-09-01

1 · Retention breakdown

curve100 samples, stored one per percent runtime32:45 gone by 0:3045.5% at halfway50% still watching methodhazard = (present before − present after) ÷ present before at each moment; baseline = mean hazard of the previous 5 moments, floored; flagged when the excess viewers lost beyond baseline ranks high; a rise is a rewind only when no comparable drop precedes it and the lift survives the next sample

Red marks are flagged drops, green are earned rewinds. Hover a mark for its note.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:00
1 · what the curve showedThe first 20 seconds drop from 100% to 59.1%, and 0:30 sits at 59.1% versus a 68.0% channel median (*-8.9pp, beats only 32 of 148*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 0:00-0:20 for a soft cold-open — greeting, framing of the three-town premise, or channel branding before any thrift find is shown. 4 · how (the next move)Trial an alternate opener that cuts to the best haul-item reveal from the three stops inside the first 8 seconds, then names the towns. 5 · rationaleThe channel's own 0:15 hold is 78.3%; this video only lags starting at 0:30, meaning the loss lands after the greeting, not on the thumbnail promise. cautionVerify no sponsor or disclosure sits in 0:00-0:20 that must remain up front; if it does, keep it and move the greeting instead.
drop3:17
1 · what the curve showedStop rate runs 1.2x the channel norm across 3:17-4:55 while audience only slips from 54.5% to 51.8% (*4.1x the surrounding rate*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 3:17-4:55 for a travel-transition or store-entry segment — driving shots, parking, or walking into the first shop before any item is examined. 4 · how (the next move)Tighten 3:17-4:55 to under 40 seconds, keeping only the storefront establishing shot and cutting straight to the first item pickup. 5 · rationaleThe drop is mild in absolute terms but flagged typical for the channel, so trimming connective tissue here recovers time without touching finds.
peak3:17
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 1.7% and holds for four samples at 54.5%, coinciding with the same window flagged as a mild stop-rate spike. 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 3:17 for a moment viewers scrubbed back to — likely a price tag being read out or a first-store item close-up worth a second look. 4 · how (the next move)Identify the exact frame drawing the rewind and lift that item or price into the intro reveal proposed for 0:00-0:08. 5 · rationaleA replay at the same timestamp as a stop-rate spike means the moment is polarising — worth surfacing earlier to hook the audience that leaves at 0:30.
peak3:56
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 3.4% to 55.5%, briefly climbing above the 1:00 mark, held for two samples. 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 3:56 for a specific find being named or a price being read — the short hold suggests a single quotable beat rather than a sustained segment. 4 · how (the next move)Pull the audio from 3:56 as a candidate for the video's cold-open teaser or the thumbnail item callout. 5 · rationaleA 3.4% lift on a low-view vlog is a genuine interest signal about the content of the moment, not the segment around it.
drop6:13
1 · what the curve showedA 20-second window loses viewers at 1.4x the channel norm (*3.4x surrounding, 51.8% down to 50.0%*), unusual for this position on the channel. 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 6:13-6:33 for a dead beat — an item put back, a price reaction that fizzles, or a cut between aisles with no commentary. 4 · how (the next move)Cut 6:13-6:33 entirely and rejoin on the next item being picked up or the next price being read aloud. 5 · rationaleThis is one of the few moments flagged not typical for the channel, so the loss is specific to this segment rather than a habitual pattern.
peak10:48
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises 11.3% and holds for 17 samples at 53.6%, by far the strongest replay signal in the video. 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 10:48 for a standout haul reveal, a surprising price, or a full-item breakdown viewers rewound to study. 4 · how (the next move)Build the next video's thumbnail and title around whatever item or moment sits at 10:48, and lead that video with it. 5 · rationaleA 17-sample hold at a 33% position is the clearest evidence of what this audience actually came for — treat it as the premise, not a mid-video beat. cautionConfirm the moment is a genuine reveal and not a chapter marker or timestamp linked from the description driving skip-to traffic.

1 · Retention breakdown

curve100 samples, stored one per percent runtime10:45 gone by 0:3033.3% at halfway56% still watching methodhazard = (present before − present after) ÷ present before at each moment; baseline = mean hazard of the previous 5 moments, floored; flagged when the excess viewers lost beyond baseline ranks high; a rise is a rewind only when no comparable drop precedes it and the lift survives the next sample

Red marks are flagged drops, green are earned rewinds. Hover a mark for its note.

2 · Each flagged moment: from curve to note

drop0:00
1 · what the curve showedThe opening six seconds shed roughly a fifth of the audience, but less than the channel's usual first-frame bleed (*6.84% stop rate versus the channel's 8.54% norm, 0.8x*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 0:00-0:06 for the standard first-frame exit as viewers judge the thumbnail-title match before any content lands. 4 · how (the next move)Keep the current cold open intact and reuse its structure on the next upload. 5 · rationaleThe opening already beats the channel's own first-frame norm and sets up a top-decile finish, so this is a template to copy, not fix.
drop0:52
1 · what the curve showedA short exit runs 1.4x the channel's usual rate here, above norm but small in absolute terms (*2.49% versus 1.73% typical, 2.1x the surrounding stop rate*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 0:52-0:58 for a setup beat or transition where the premise is restated before the first real development. 4 · how (the next move)Trial trimming 0:52-0:58 into the beat that follows and cutting to the next concrete moment. 5 · rationaleRemoving a soft restatement here should tighten the run into the 1:00 mark, where the video already crosses above the channel median. cautionCannot confirm from data alone whether this beat sets up a later payoff — verify before cutting and keep it if a callback depends on it.
drop1:37
1 · what the curve showedA thirteen-second stretch loses less audience than the channel usually loses at this position (*0.76% stop rate versus 1.19% typical, 0.6x the channel norm*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 1:37-1:50 for the channel's standing habit of a mid-intro sag — this video handles it better than most. 4 · how (the next move)Leave 1:37-1:50 as edited and study its pacing when cutting future intros. 5 · rationaleThe spike ratio flags it locally, but against the channel it under-loses, so intervention would risk breaking what works.
peak2:09
1 · what the curve showedAudience rises here and holds for eight samples, the longest sustained lift in the video (*3.8% of the audience present, held for 8 samples, 62.1% still watching*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 2:09 for a reveal, admission, or first concrete detail viewers rewound to catch after the intro beats. 4 · how (the next move)Front-load a beat of the same shape into the first sixty seconds of the next upload. 5 · rationaleAn eight-sample hold this early is the strongest interest signal in the video and should be the model for future opens.
peak5:10
1 · what the curve showedA brief lift at the halfway mark holds for three samples as the video crosses the channel's median line (*2.1% of the audience present, 56.3% still watching*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 5:10 for a turn, decision, or new piece of information landing where most of the channel's videos have already sagged. 4 · how (the next move)Tighten the sixty seconds preceding 5:10 so the turn lands sooner in future cuts of similar material. 5 · rationaleThe video is already 5.1pp above channel median at 5:00, so accelerating into this beat compounds the advantage.
peak9:15
1 · what the curve showedAudience ticks up in the final stretch and holds for three samples, unusual this close to an outro (*2.4% of the audience present, 48.3% still watching at 86% through*). 2 · evidence at that secondno transcript line available; the note uses check-this-timestamp language 3 · why (the check or the quote)Check 9:15 for a late resolution or closing admission viewers scrubbed back to hear once they realised the video was ending. 4 · how (the next move)Preserve the exact cut from 9:15 to the end and reuse this closing shape on similar videos. 5 · rationaleThis video ranks 1 of 149 for audience-at-end on the channel, and this late lift is the specific behaviour driving that finish.
